<details type="tool_calls" done="true" id="chatcmpl-tool-8c1b4864bc9d3461" name="docgen_write" arguments="&quot;{\&quot;request\&quot;: \&quot;{\\\&quot;format\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;pdf\\\&quot;, \\\&quot;filename\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;Radioactive Isotopes\\\&quot;, \\\&quot;content\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;# Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n\\\\n## A Comprehensive Guide\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Table of Contents\\\\n\\\\n1. Introduction to Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n2. Atomic Structure and Nuclear Stability\\\\n3. Types of Radioactive Decay\\\\n4. Half-Life and Decay Kinetics\\\\n5. Natural Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n6. Artificial (Synthetic) Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n7. Radioactive Isotopes in Medicine\\\\n8. Industrial and Agricultural Applications\\\\n9. Dating and Archaeology\\\\n10. Nuclear Power and Energy\\\\n11. Radiation Safety and Protection\\\\n12. Environmental Impact and Radioactive Waste\\\\n13. Famous Radioactive Isotopes \\u2014 A Reference\\\\n14. Glossary\\\\n15. Further Reading\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 1 \\u2014 Introduction to Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n\\\\n## What Are Isotopes?\\\\n\\\\nEvery chemical element is defined by its atomic number \\u2014 the number of protons in its nucleus. For example, every atom of carbon has exactly 6 protons. But atoms of the same element can differ in how many neutrons they carry. These variants are called **isotopes**.\\\\n\\\\nCarbon, for instance, has three naturally occurring isotopes:\\\\n\\\\n- **Carbon-12** (6 protons, 6 neutrons) \\u2014 the most abundant, stable\\\\n- **Carbon-13** (6 protons, 7 neutrons) \\u2014 stable, makes up about 1.1% of natural carbon\\\\n- **Carbon-14** (6 protons, 8 neutrons) \\u2014 unstable, radioactive, present in trace amounts\\\\n\\\\nThe first two are stable; they will never spontaneously change. Carbon-14, however, is **radioactive**: its nucleus is unstable and will eventually break apart, releasing energy in the process.\\\\n\\\\n## Radioactivity \\u2014 The Core Idea\\\\n\\\\n**Radioactivity** is the spontaneous emission of particles or electromagnetic radiation from an unstable atomic nucleus. The term was coined by Marie Curie, derived from the Latin *radius* (ray), in recognition of the penetrating rays emitted by uranium and thorium salts.\\\\n\\\\nIsotopes that undergo radioactivity are called **radioisotopes** or **radionuclides**. Of the roughly 3,300 known nuclides (distinct combinations of protons and neutrons), only about 250\\u2013270 are truly stable. The rest are radioactive, decaying over timescales ranging from fractions of a second to billions of years.\\\\n\\\\n## Why Do Nuclei Become Unstable?\\\\n\\\\nA nucleus stays together because of the **strong nuclear force** \\u2014 an immensely powerful but very short-range attraction between nucleons (protons and neutrons). It competes against the **electromagnetic repulsion** between positively charged protons. The balance between these forces determines stability.\\\\n\\\\n- If a nucleus has too many or too few neutrons relative to protons, it is unbalanced and radioactive.\\\\n- Very heavy nuclei (beyond lead, atomic number 82) cannot hold together stably regardless of the neutron-to-proton ratio.\\\\n\\\\nThe range of stable nuclei is called the **band of stability** on a chart of neutrons versus protons. Radioactive isotopes lie outside this band and decay to move toward it.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 2 \\u2014 Atomic Structure and Nuclear Stability\\\\n\\\\n## The Nucleus in Detail\\\\n\\\\nThe atomic nucleus sits at the center of an atom, packed with protons and neutrons collectively called **nucleons**. Key facts:\\\\n\\\\n- The nucleus occupies less than one ten-thousandth of an atom&#x27;s diameter but contains over 99.9% of its mass.\\\\n- Nuclear densities reach approximately $2.3 \\\\\\\\times 10^{17}$ kg/m\\u00b3 \\u2014 a sugar-cube-sized sample of nuclear matter would weigh roughly two hundred million tons.\\\\n\\\\n## Binding Energy\\\\n\\\\nWhen nucleons bind together, energy is released. The **binding energy** is the energy required to completely separate a nucleus into individual protons and neutrons. Equivalently, it is the energy released when the nucleus forms. This comes from the mass defect \\u2014 the mass of a bound nucleus is slightly less than the sum of its parts, with the missing mass converted to energy via $E = mc^2$.\\\\n\\\\nThe **binding energy per nucleon** peaks near iron-56, making iron the most tightly bound element. Elements lighter than iron can release energy through fusion; elements heavier than iron can release energy through fission.\\\\n\\\\n## The Band of Stability\\\\n\\\\nFor light elements (up to calcium, Z = 20), stable isotopes tend to have roughly equal numbers of protons and neutrons. As atomic number increases, more neutrons are needed to offset the growing proton-proton repulsion. By the time we reach lead (Z = 82), stable isotopes have nearly 1.5 neutrons per proton.\\\\n\\\\nElements beyond bismuth (Z = 83) have **no stable isotopes whatsoever**. All isotopes of polonium, radon, radium, uranium, plutonium, and all elements beyond are radioactive.\\\\n\\\\n## Magic Numbers\\\\n\\\\nCertain numbers of protons or neutrons \\u2014 **2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, and 126** \\u2014 confer extra stability, analogous to the electron shell closures that make noble gases unreactive. Nuclei with both a magic number of protons and a magic number of neutrons are called **doubly magic** and are exceptionally stable (e.g., helium-4, oxygen-16, calcium-40, lead-208).\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 3 \\u2014 Types of Radioactive Decay\\\\n\\\\nUnstable nuclei reach stability through several distinct decay modes. Each produces characteristic radiation.\\\\n\\\\n## Alpha ($\\\\\\\\alpha$) Decay\\\\n\\\\nAn alpha particle is a helium-4 nucleus: two protons and two neutrons bound tightly together. In alpha decay, a heavy nucleus ejects an alpha particle:\\\\n\\\\n$$^{238}_{92}\\\\\\\\text{U} \\\\\\\\rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\\\\\\\\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\\\\\\\\text{He}$$\\\\n\\\\n**Properties:**\\\\n- Alpha particles are heavy, slow, and doubly charged.\\\\n- They have very low penetration \\u2014 stopped by a sheet of paper or the outer layer of skin.\\\\n- If inhaled or ingested, however, they are extremely damaging because they deposit a large amount of energy in a short range.\\\\n\\\\n## Beta ($\\\\\\\\beta$) Decay\\\\n\\\\nBeta decay involves the weak nuclear force and changes a neutron into a proton (or vice versa):\\\\n\\\\n### Beta-minus ($\\\\\\\\beta^-$) Decay\\\\nA neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino:\\\\n\\\\n$$^{14}_{6}\\\\\\\\text{C} \\\\\\\\rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\\\\\\\\text{N} + e^- + \\\\\\\\bar{\\\\\\\\nu}_e$$\\\\n\\\\n### Beta-plus ($\\\\\\\\beta^+$) Decay (Positron Emission)\\\\nA proton converts to a neutron, emitting a positron and a neutrino:\\\\n\\\\n$$^{22}_{11}\\\\\\\\text{Na} \\\\\\\\rightarrow {}^{22}_{10}\\\\\\\\text{Ne} + e^+ + \\\\\\\\nu_e$$\\\\n\\\\n**Properties:**\\\\n- Electrons and positrons are light and moderately penetrating.\\\\n- A few millimeters of aluminum will stop most beta particles.\\\\n- Beta-minus is common among neutron-rich isotopes; beta-plus among proton-rich ones.\\\\n\\\\n## Gamma ($\\\\\\\\gamma$) Decay\\\\n\\\\nGamma rays are high-energy photons emitted when an excited nucleus drops to a lower energy state. Gamma decay often accompanies alpha or beta decay, as the daughter nucleus is frequently left in an excited state:\\\\n\\\\n$$^{60}_{27}\\\\\\\\text{Co}^* \\\\\\\\rightarrow {}^{60}_{27}\\\\\\\\text{Co} + \\\\\\\\gamma$$\\\\n\\\\n**Properties:**\\\\n- Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than X-rays.\\\\n- They are highly penetrating \\u2014 requiring thick lead or meters of concrete for effective shielding.\\\\n- Gamma decay does not change the number of protons or neutrons.\\\\n\\\\n## Electron Capture\\\\n\\\\nA nucleus captures one of its own inner-shell electrons, converting a proton to a neutron:\\\\n\\\\n$$^{7}_{4}\\\\\\\\text{Be} + e^- \\\\\\\\rightarrow {}^{7}_{3}\\\\\\\\text{Li} + \\\\\\\\nu_e$$\\\\n\\\\nThis leaves a vacancy in the inner electron shell, producing characteristic X-rays when outer electrons cascade down.\\\\n\\\\n## Spontaneous Fission\\\\n\\\\nVery heavy nuclei (e.g., californium-252) can split into two roughly equal fragments, releasing several free neutrons and enormous energy. This is the same basic process exploited in nuclear weapons and reactors, occurring spontaneously in rare cases.\\\\n\\\\n## Comparison Table\\\\n\\\\n| Decay Type | Particle Emitted | Charge | Penetration | Stopped By |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Alpha ($\\\\\\\\alpha$) | Helium nucleus | +2 | Very low | Paper, skin |\\\\n| Beta-minus ($\\\\\\\\beta^-$) | Electron | -1 | Moderate | Aluminum foil |\\\\n| Beta-plus ($\\\\\\\\beta^+$) | Positron | +1 | Moderate | Aluminum foil |\\\\n| Gamma ($\\\\\\\\gamma$) | Photon | 0 | Very high | Lead, concrete |\\\\n| Neutron | Neutron | 0 | Very high | Water, concrete |\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 4 \\u2014 Half-Life and Decay Kinetics\\\\n\\\\n## The Half-Life Concept\\\\n\\\\nThe **half-life** ($t_{1/2}$) of a radioactive isotope is the time required for half of a sample of that isotope to decay. It is a fixed property of each radionuclide, unaffected by temperature, pressure, chemical state, or virtually any other environmental factor.\\\\n\\\\nHalf-lives range wildly:\\\\n\\\\n- **Polonium-214**: 164 microseconds\\\\n- **Iodine-131**: 8.02 days\\\\n- **Carbon-14**: 5,730 years\\\\n- **Uranium-238**: 4.47 billion years\\\\n- **Tellurium-128**: $2.2 \\\\\\\\times 10^{24}$ years (longer than the age of the universe)\\\\n\\\\n## The Decay Law\\\\n\\\\nThe number of radioactive nuclei remaining after time $t$ follows an exponential law:\\\\n\\\\n$$N(t) = N_0 \\\\\\\\cdot \\\\\\\\left(\\\\\\\\frac{1}{2}\\\\\\\\right)^{t / t_{1/2}}$$\\\\n\\\\nwhere $N_0$ is the initial number and $N(t)$ is the number remaining.\\\\n\\\\nEquivalently, the **decay constant** $\\\\\\\\lambda = \\\\\\\\ln(2) / t_{1/2}$ relates to the activity:\\\\n\\\\n$$A(t) = \\\\\\\\lambda \\\\\\\\cdot N(t)$$\\\\n\\\\nwhere **Activity** ($A$) is the number of decays per second, measured in **becquerels (Bq)**. One becquerel equals one decay per second. The older unit, the **curie (Ci)**, equals $3.7 \\\\\\\\times 10^{10}$ Bq \\u2014 originally defined as the activity of one gram of radium-226.\\\\n\\\\n## Decay Chains\\\\n\\\\nMany isotopes do not decay directly to a stable product. Instead, they decay through a **chain** of intermediate radioactive isotopes. The uranium-238 series, for example, involves 14 steps (8 alpha decays and 6 beta decays) before reaching stable lead-206:\\\\n\\\\nUranium-238 \\u2192 Thorium-234 \\u2192 Protactinium-234 \\u2192 Uranium-234 \\u2192 ... \\u2192 Lead-206 (stable)\\\\n\\\\nThese chains produce a mixture of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation, and intermediate products can separate from the parent and migrate through the environment.\\\\n\\\\n## Secular Equilibrium\\\\n\\\\nIn a decay chain, when the parent isotope&#x27;s half-life is enormously longer than any daughter&#x27;s, the daughters eventually reach a steady production rate equal to their decay rate. At **secular equilibrium**, the activity of every member of the chain equals the activity of the parent. This principle is important in radiation measurement and in understanding natural radiation exposure.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 5 \\u2014 Natural Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n\\\\n## Primordial Radionuclides\\\\n\\\\nSome radioactive isotopes were formed in supernovae before the birth of our solar system and have survived to the present because of their extremely long half-lives. The three most significant primordial decay chains are:\\\\n\\\\n1. **The Uranium Series** (starting with U-238, $t_{1/2}$ = 4.47 billion years)\\\\n2. **The Actinium Series** (starting with U-235, $t_{1/2}$ = 704 million years)\\\\n3. **The Thorium Series** (starting with Th-232, $t_{1/2}$ = 14.05 billion years)\\\\n\\\\nOther primordial radionuclides include:\\\\n- **Potassium-40** ($t_{1/2}$ = 1.25 billion years) \\u2014 present in all living things, in bananas, in granite\\\\n- **Rubidium-87** ($t_{1/2}$ = 48.8 billion years)\\\\n- **Lutetium-176** ($t_{1/2}$ = 37 billion years)\\\\n\\\\n## Cosmogenic Radionuclides\\\\n\\\\nThese are created continuously by cosmic rays striking atoms in the Earth&#x27;s atmosphere or surface:\\\\n\\\\n- **Carbon-14** \\u2014 produced when cosmic-ray neutrons hit nitrogen-14\\\\n- **Tritium (H-3)** \\u2014 produced by neutron capture on lithium and other reactions\\\\n- **Beryllium-10** \\u2014 produced in the upper atmosphere, used to date geological formations\\\\n- **Aluminum-26** and **Chlorine-36** \\u2014 produced by spallation reactions\\\\n\\\\n## Radiogenic Radionuclides\\\\n\\\\nThese arise as decay products of the primordial isotopes:\\\\n\\\\n- **Radon-222** \\u2014 a colorless, odorless radioactive gas produced from radium-226 in the uranium series. It can accumulate in homes and is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking.\\\\n- **Polonium-210** \\u2014 part of the uranium-238 decay chain, highly toxic\\\\n- **Radon-220** (thoron) \\u2014 from the thorium series\\\\n\\\\n## Background Radiation\\\\n\\\\nEvery person on Earth receives a continuous dose of natural radiation:\\\\n\\\\n- **Cosmic radiation** from space (higher at altitude)\\\\n- **Terrestrial radiation** from uranium, thorium, and potassium in soil and rock\\\\n- **Internal radiation** from K-40 and C-14 within the body\\\\n- **Radon inhalation** \\u2014 the largest single source of natural exposure for most people\\\\n\\\\nThe global average natural background dose is approximately **2.4 mSv per year**, but it can be much higher in places with high radon or monazite sands (e.g., Kerala, India; Guarapari, Brazil).\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 6 \\u2014 Artificial (Synthetic) Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n\\\\n## How We Make Them\\\\n\\\\nArtificial radioisotopes are produced through three main methods:\\\\n\\\\n### 1. Nuclear Reactors\\\\nNeutrons from fission bombard stable target materials, inducing neutron capture. Examples:\\\\n- Cobalt-59 \\u2192 Cobalt-60 (neutron capture)\\\\n- Iodine is produced from tellurium targets\\\\n- Tritium from lithium targets\\\\n\\\\n### 2. Particle Accelerators (Cyclotrons)\\\\nCharged particles (protons, deuterons, alpha particles) accelerate to high energies and strike target nuclei:\\\\n- Fluorine-18 (for PET scans) from oxygen-18 targets bombarded with protons\\\\n- Technetium-99m precursors\\\\n- Indium-111 for imaging\\\\n\\\\n### 3. Fission Product Separation\\\\nThe fission of uranium-235 or plutonium-239 produces a broad spectrum of neutron-rich isotopes. Useful isotopes are chemically separated from spent fuel:\\\\n- Cesium-137\\\\n- Strontium-90\\\\n- Iodine-131\\\\n\\\\n## Transuranic Elements\\\\n\\\\nElements beyond uranium (Z &gt; 92) are all synthetic and radioactive. They were created by bombarding heavy targets with neutrons or light ions. Notable examples:\\\\n\\\\n| Element | Symbol | Z | Discovery | Key Isotope |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Neptunium | Np | 93 | 1940 | Np-237 |\\\\n| Plutonium | Pu | 94 | 1940 | Pu-239 |\\\\n| Americium | Am | 95 | 1944 | Am-241 |\\\\n| Curium | Cm | 96 | 1944 | Cm-244 |\\\\n| Californium | Cf | 98 | 1950 | Cf-252 |\\\\n| Einsteinium | Es | 99 | 1952 | Es-253 |\\\\n| Fermium | Fm | 100 | 1952 | Fm-257 |\\\\n\\\\nThe heaviest elements (up to oganesson, Z = 118) have been synthesized in particle accelerators, with half-lives measured in milliseconds.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 7 \\u2014 Radioactive Isotopes in Medicine\\\\n\\\\nMedicine is the largest and most impactful application of radioisotopes, spanning diagnosis, treatment, and sterilization.\\\\n\\\\n## Diagnostic Imaging\\\\n\\\\n### Technetium-99m ($t_{1/2}$ = 6 hours)\\\\nTechnetium-99m is the workhorse of nuclear medicine, used in roughly 80% of all diagnostic nuclear imaging procedures. It decays by emitting a 140 keV gamma ray \\u2014 ideal for detection \\u2014 with no accompanying beta radiation to harm the patient. Chelated to different molecules, it can image the heart, bones, lungs, kidneys, brain, and more.\\\\n\\\\n### Fluorine-18 ($t_{1/2}$ = 110 minutes)\\\\nFluorine-18 is the key isotope in **PET (positron emission tomography)**. Attached to glucose as FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose), it allows clinicians to visualize areas of high metabolic activity \\u2014 including tumors, which greedily consume sugar.\\\\n\\\\n### Iodine-123 ($t_{1/2}$ = 13.2 hours)\\\\nUsed to image and assess thyroid function. Iodine is naturally concentrated in the thyroid, making it an ideal target.\\\\n\\\\n## Radiation Therapy\\\\n\\\\n### Iodine-131 ($t_{1/2}$ = 8 days)\\\\nAdministered orally to destroy overactive thyroid tissue (Graves&#x27; disease) or thyroid cancer. The thyroid&#x27;s natural iodine uptake concentrates the radiation where it is needed.\\\\n\\\\n### Cobalt-60 ($t_{1/2}$ = 5.27 years)\\\\nThe Cobalt-60 teletherapy machine (\\\\\\\&quot;Cobalt bomb\\\\\\\&quot;) was the first form of external beam radiation therapy. Though largely replaced by linear accelerators, it remains in use in many developing countries due to its ruggedness and lower cost.\\\\n\\\\n### Phosphorus-32 ($t_{1/2}$ = 14.3 days)\\\\nUsed to treat polycythemia vera and certain forms of leukemia by targeting rapidly dividing blood cells.\\\\n\\\\n### Strontium-89 and Samarium-153\\\\nAdministered intravenously to treat bone metastases. Both are calcium mimics that accumulate in areas of high bone turnover, delivering localized radiation to painful tumor sites.\\\\n\\\\n### Brachytherapy\\\\nSealed radioactive sources are placed directly inside or next to the tumor:\\\\n- **Iridium-192** \\u2014 for breast, cervix, and prostate cancer\\\\n- **Iodine-125** \\u2014 permanently implanted seeds for prostate cancer\\\\n- **Radium-223** (Xofigo) \\u2014 an alpha-emitter for bone metastases from prostate cancer\\\\n\\\\n## Sterilization\\\\n\\\\nCobalt-60 and cesium-137 gamma sources sterilize medical equipment (syringes, surgical gloves, sutures, implants) that would be damaged by heat. The radiation destroys DNA in microorganisms, rendering them non-viable. Over 40% of the world&#x27;s single-use medical devices are sterilized this way.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 8 \\u2014 Industrial and Agricultural Applications\\\\n\\\\n## Industrial Radiography\\\\n\\\\nGamma sources (iridium-192, cobalt-60) or X-ray machines inspect welds, pipelines, aircraft structures, and castings for internal flaws, much as X-rays image the human body. This is far more reliable than visual inspection for hidden defects.\\\\n\\\\n## Thickness and Density Gauges\\\\n\\\\nBeta or gamma sources measure the thickness of moving material in real time:\\\\n- Paper mills use beta emitters to control paper thickness\\\\n- Steel mills use gamma sources to measure hot rolling\\\\n- Petroleum industry uses neutron and gamma gauges to analyze soil and rock density during drilling\\\\n\\\\n## Smoke Detectors\\\\n\\\\nAmericium-241 (alpha emitter) ionizes air in a detection chamber. Smoke particles disrupt the ion current, triggering the alarm. Roughly one billion such detectors contain trace amounts of Am-241.\\\\n\\\\n## Tracers\\\\n\\\\nRadioactive tracers track the flow of fluids through pipelines, detect leaks, and study mixing processes. Because even tiny amounts of radioisotopes are easily detected, they provide sensitive, real-time tracking without disrupting the system.\\\\n\\\\n## Agriculture\\\\n\\\\n### Mutation Breeding\\\\nControlled irradiation with cobalt-60 gamma rays induces random mutations in plant seeds. Thousands of crop varieties \\u2014 including disease-resistant wheat, drought-tolerant sorghum, and higher-yield rice \\u2014 have been developed this way.\\\\n\\\\n### Pest Control (Sterile Insect Technique)\\\\nMale insects (e.g., medfly, tsetse fly, screwworm) are reared in massive facilities, sterilized with radiation, and released in huge numbers. Because they cannot reproduce, the wild population crashes. This technique has eradicated screwworm from the Americas.\\\\n\\\\n### Food Irradiation\\\\nLow-dose gamma or electron beam irradiation kills bacteria, parasites, and insects in food without making the food radioactive. Approved foods include spices, fruits, vegetables, and meats. Irradiation extends shelf life and reduces foodborne illness.\\\\n\\\\n### Fertilizer Uptake Studies\\\\nPhosphorus-32 and other tracers track how plants absorb and distribute nutrients, helping optimize fertilizer application.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 9 \\u2014 Dating and Archaeology\\\\n\\\\n## Carbon-14 Dating (Radiocarbon Dating)\\\\n\\\\nDiscovered by Willard Libby in 1949, carbon-14 dating revolutionized archaeology. Living organisms continuously exchange carbon with the atmosphere, maintaining a steady ratio of C-14 to C-12. At death, the exchange stops and C-14 decays with a half-life of 5,730 years.\\\\n\\\\n$$\\\\\\\\text{Age} = -\\\\\\\\frac{t_{1/2}}{\\\\\\\\ln(2)} \\\\\\\\cdot \\\\\\\\ln\\\\\\\\left(\\\\\\\\frac{N}{N_0}\\\\\\\\right)$$\\\\n\\\\nThe method is reliable up to about 50,000\\u201360,000 years (roughly 10 half-lives). Beyond that, too little C-14 remains to measure accurately.\\\\n\\\\n**Calibration** is required because the atmospheric C-14/C-12 ratio has varied over time. Tree-ring dating (dendrochronology) and ice core records provide the calibration curve.\\\\n\\\\n## Uranium-Lead Dating\\\\n\\\\nUranium-238 decays to lead-206 over 4.47 billion years, and uranium-235 decays to lead-206 over 704 million years. Measuring both ratios in a mineral like zircon gives a robust age \\u2014 one of the methods used to date the Earth itself at approximately 4.54 billion years.\\\\n\\\\n## Potassium-Argon Dating\\\\n\\\\nPotassium-40 ($t_{1/2}$ = 1.25 billion years) decays to argon-40, a gas that escapes molten rock but gets trapped when lava solidifies. The method dates volcanic rocks from about 100,000 years to the age of the Earth, and is essential for dating early hominin sites in East Africa.\\\\n\\\\n## Other Methods\\\\n\\\\n| Method | Isotope | Half-Life | Useful Range |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Carbon-14 | C-14 | 5,730 years | Up to ~50,000 years |\\\\n| Potassium-Argon | K-40 | 1.25 billion years | 100 ka \\u2013 Earth&#x27;s age |\\\\n| Uranium-Lead | U-238 / U-235 | 4.47 Ga / 0.704 Ga | Millions \\u2013 billions of years |\\\\n| Rubidium-Strontium | Rb-87 | 48.8 billion years | Billions of years |\\\\n| Lutetium-Hafnium | Lu-176 | 37 billion years | Billions of years |\\\\n| Beryllium-10 | Be-10 | 1.39 million years | Exposure dating of surfaces |\\\\n| Chlorine-36 | Cl-36 | 301,000 years | Groundwater dating |\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 10 \\u2014 Nuclear Power and Energy\\\\n\\\\n## Fission Energy\\\\n\\\\nNuclear power plants split heavy nuclei \\u2014 primarily uranium-235 ($t_{1/2}$ = 704 million years) and plutonium-239 ($t_{1/2}$ = 24,110 years) \\u2014 releasing enormous energy. Each fission event liberates approximately 200 MeV of energy, roughly a million times the energy released in a chemical reaction.\\\\n\\\\n### The Fuel Cycle\\\\nNatural uranium contains only 0.7% U-235 (fissile); the rest is U-238 (fertile). Most reactors require enrichment to 3\\u20135% U-235. In the reactor, U-238 also captures neutrons to form Pu-239, which itself undergoes fission.\\\\n\\\\n### Breeder Reactors\\\\nFast breeder reactors convert fertile isotopes (U-238, Th-232) into fissile fuel (Pu-239, U-233), potentially extending uranium resources by a factor of 60 or more. Thorium (Th-232) is abundant and produces U-233 as fissile fuel, but the technology remains largely experimental.\\\\n\\\\n## Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators (RTGs)\\\\n\\\\nRTGs convert the heat from radioactive decay directly into electricity using thermocouples. **Plutonium-238** ($t_{1/2}$ = 87.7 years, alpha emitter) is the standard RTG fuel.\\\\n\\\\nRTGs power:\\\\n- Voyager 1 and 2 (launched 1977, still operating at over 15 billion km)\\\\n- New Horizons (Pluto flyby 2015, still active)\\\\n- Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers\\\\n- InSight Mars lander\\\\n- Deep Space 1, Cassini, Galileo, and many other missions\\\\n\\\\nRTGs can operate for decades in environments where solar panels are impractical: deep space, the Martian winter, or the dark side of the Moon.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 11 \\u2014 Radiation Safety and Protection\\\\n\\\\n## Dose and Measurement\\\\n\\\\nUnderstanding radiation requires distinguishing between exposure, absorbed dose, and effective dose:\\\\n\\\\n| Quantity | Unit | Description |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| Activity | Bq (becquerel) | Decays per second |\\\\n| Absorbed dose | Gy (gray) | Energy deposited per kg (1 Gy = 1 J/kg) |\\\\n| Equivalent dose | Sv (sievert) | Absorbed dose \\u00d7 radiation weighting factor |\\\\n| Effective dose | Sv | Equivalent dose \\u00d7 tissue weighting factor |\\\\n\\\\nThe **sievert** accounts for the fact that alpha particles cause more biological damage than beta or gamma radiation per unit of energy absorbed.\\\\n\\\\n### Typical Doses\\\\n\\\\n| Source | Effective Dose |\\\\n|---|---|\\\\n| Background radiation (annual) | ~2.4 mSv |\\\\n| Chest X-ray | 0.1 mSv |\\\\n| CT scan (abdomen) | ~10 mSv |\\\\n| Dental X-ray | 0.005 mSv |\\\\n| Cross-country flight | 0.1 mSv |\\\\n| Annual occupational limit (workers) | 50 mSv |\\\\n| Acute whole-body dose causing illness | ~1,000 mSv (1 Sv) |\\\\n| Lethal dose (LD50, 60 days) | ~3,500\\u20134,000 mSv |\\\\n\\\\n## The ALARA Principle\\\\n\\\\nRadiation protection is guided by **ALARA**: *As Low As Reasonably Achievable*. Three practical principles:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Time** \\u2014 minimize the duration of exposure\\\\n2. **Distance** \\u2014 radiation intensity falls with the square of the distance (inverse square law)\\\\n3. **Shielding** \\u2014 interpose appropriate material (lead for gamma, plastic for beta, water/concrete for neutrons)\\\\n\\\\n## Regulatory Limits\\\\n\\\\nMost countries limit public exposure from artificial sources to 1 mSv per year (above background). Nuclear workers are typically limited to 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years, with no more than 50 mSv in any single year.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 12 \\u2014 Environmental Impact and Radioactive Waste\\\\n\\\\n## Categories of Waste\\\\n\\\\n| Category | Examples | Management |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| Low-level waste | Gloves, tools, filters | Near-surface disposal |\\\\n| Intermediate-level waste | Resins, chemical sludges | Concrete encapsulation, intermediate depth |\\\\n| High-level waste | Spent nuclear fuel | Deep geological repositories |\\\\n| Transuranic waste | Plutonium-bearing materials | Deep disposal (e.g., WIPP, USA) |\\\\n\\\\n## Spent Nuclear Fuel\\\\n\\\\nEach year the world&#x27;s nuclear reactors produce roughly 10,000\\u201312,000 tons of spent fuel. It remains highly radioactive and thermally hot for thousands of years. After decades of cooling in spent fuel pools, dry cask storage extends the cooling period. Deep geological repositories (e.g., Onkalo in Finland, expected to open ~2025) are the long-term solution.\\\\n\\\\n## Historical Disasters\\\\n\\\\n### Chernobyl (1986)\\\\nA design flaw and operator error caused an uncontrolled power surge and steam explosion at Reactor 4 of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine. The reactor core was exposed, catching fire and releasing an estimated 5% of its inventory of radioactive material \\u2014 the equivalent of roughly 400 times the radiation released at Hiroshima. Approximately 6 million people received some additional radiation exposure.\\\\n\\\\n### Fukushima Daiichi (2011)\\\\nA massive earthquake and tsunami disabled cooling systems at three reactors, leading to meltdowns and hydrogen explosions. About 10\\u201320% of the Chernobyl release was emitted. The surrounding area was evacuated and remains partially restricted.\\\\n\\\\n### Three Mile Island (1979)\\\\nA partial meltdown at a reactor in Pennsylvania released small amounts of radioactivity. No direct deaths occurred, but it significantly shaped U.S. nuclear policy.\\\\n\\\\n## Nuclear Weapons Legacy\\\\n\\\\nWeapons testing between 1945 and 1980 released significant radioactive material into the atmosphere, particularly strontium-90 and cesium-137, which are now detectable worldwide. Fall-out concentrations are low but measurable, and some test sites (e.g., Nevada Test Site, Semipalatinsk in Kazakhstan) remain contaminated.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 13 \\u2014 Famous Radioactive Isotopes \\u2014 A Reference\\\\n\\\\n| Isotope | Symbol | Half-Life | Decay Mode | Key Applications |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Tritium | H-3 | 12.3 years | \\u03b2\\u207b | Self-luminous sights, fusion research |\\\\n| Carbon-14 | C-14 | 5,730 years | \\u03b2\\u207b | Radiocarbon dating, biochemical tracers |\\\\n| Potassium-40 | K-40 | 1.25 billion years | \\u03b2\\u207b, EC | Geological dating, natural background |\\\\n| Cobalt-60 | Co-60 | 5.27 years | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Cancer therapy, sterilization, radiography |\\\\n| Cesium-137 | Cs-137 | 30.17 years | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Medical therapy, industrial gauges |\\\\n| Strontium-90 | Sr-90 | 28.8 years | \\u03b2\\u207b | RTGs, bone pain palliation |\\\\n| Iodine-131 | I-131 | 8.02 days | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Thyroid treatment and diagnosis |\\\\n| Technetium-99m | Tc-99m | 6 hours | \\u03b3 | Diagnostic imaging (most common) |\\\\n| Americium-241 | Am-241 | 432.2 years | \\u03b1 + \\u03b3 | Smoke detectors |\\\\n| Plutonium-238 | Pu-238 | 87.7 years | \\u03b1 | RTGs for space missions |\\\\n| Plutonium-239 | Pu-239 | 24,110 years | \\u03b1 | Nuclear weapons, reactor fuel |\\\\n| Radium-226 | Ra-226 | 1,600 years | \\u03b1 + \\u03b3 | Historical luminescent paint, cancer therapy |\\\\n| Radon-222 | Rn-222 | 3.82 days | \\u03b1 | Natural hazard in buildings |\\\\n| Polonium-210 | Po-210 | 138.4 days | \\u03b1 | Static eliminators, historical poison |\\\\n| Californium-252 | Cf-252 | 2.645 years | \\u03b1, SF | Neutron source, oil well logging |\\\\n| Uranium-235 | U-235 | 704 million years | \\u03b1 | Nuclear fuel, weapons |\\\\n| Uranium-238 | U-238 | 4.47 billion years | \\u03b1 | Fertile material, depleted uranium |\\\\n| Thorium-232 | Th-232 | 14.05 billion years | \\u03b1 | Potential nuclear fuel |\\\\n| Fluorine-18 | F-18 | 110 minutes | \\u03b2\\u207a | PET imaging (FDG) |\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 14 \\u2014 Glossary\\\\n\\\\n**Activity** \\u2014 The number of nuclear decays per unit time, measured in becquerels (Bq).\\\\n\\\\n**Alpha particle** \\u2014 A helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons), emitted in alpha decay.\\\\n\\\\n**Band of stability** \\u2014 The region on a chart of neutron number vs. proton number where stable nuclides are found.\\\\n\\\\n**Becquerel (Bq)** \\u2014 The SI unit of radioactivity; one decay per second.\\\\n\\\\n**Binding energy** \\u2014 The energy required to disassemble a nucleus into its constituent nucleons.\\\\n\\\\n**Brachytherapy** \\u2014 Radiation therapy using sealed sources placed inside or adjacent to the target tissue.\\\\n\\\\n**Curie (Ci)** \\u2014 An older unit of activity; 1 Ci = $3.7 \\\\\\\\times 10^{10}$ Bq.\\\\n\\\\n**Decay chain** \\u2014 A sequence of successive radioactive decays from a parent isotope to a stable product.\\\\n\\\\n**Decay constant ($\\\\\\\\lambda$)** \\u2014 The probability per unit time that a given nucleus will decay.\\\\n\\\\n**Effective dose** \\u2014 A weighted sum of equivalent doses to different tissues, measured in sieverts.\\\\n\\\\n**Fission** \\u2014 The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy.\\\\n\\\\n**Fusion** \\u2014 The combining of light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.\\\\n\\\\n**Gray (Gy)** \\u2014 The SI unit of absorbed dose; 1 Gy = 1 joule per kilogram.\\\\n\\\\n**Half-life** \\u2014 The time for half of a radioactive sample to decay.\\\\n\\\\n**Isotope** \\u2014 Atoms of the same element (same proton number) with different neutron numbers.\\\\n\\\\n**Mass defect** \\u2014 The difference between the sum of a nucleus&#x27;s individual nucleon masses and its actual mass.\\\\n\\\\n**Radioisotope / Radionuclide** \\u2014 A radioactive isotope.\\\\n\\\\n**Sievert (Sv)** \\u2014 The SI unit of equivalent and effective dose, accounting for radiation type and tissue sensitivity.\\\\n\\\\n**Strong nuclear force** \\u2014 The fundamental force binding nucleons together.\\\\n\\\\n**Transmutation** \\u2014 The conversion of one element or isotope into another through nuclear reactions.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 15 \\u2014 Further Reading\\\\n\\\\n## Books\\\\n- *The Disintegration of the Elements* \\u2014 Ernest Rutherford (1904)\\\\n- *Atoms for Peace and War* \\u2014 John M. McPhee\\\\n- *The Making of the Atomic Bomb* \\u2014 Richard Rhodes\\\\n- *Radiation: A Love Story* \\u2014 Helen Caldicott\\\\n- *Nuclear Physics: Principles and Applications* \\u2014 John S. M. Geselowitz\\\\n\\\\n## Online Resources\\\\n- International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) \\u2014 www.iaea.org\\\\n- U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NLR) \\u2014 www.nrc.gov\\\\n- Radionuclide Properties Database \\u2014 https://wwwndc.jaea.go.jp/\\\\n- Interactive Table of Nuclides \\u2014 https://periodictable.com/properties/radioactivity/radioactivity.html\\\\n\\\\n## Journals\\\\n- *Journal of Nuclear Medicine*\\\\n- *Health Physics*\\\\n- *Radiation Protection Dosimetry*\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n*This book is intended for educational purposes. Always consult licensed professionals for medical, industrial, or safety decisions involving radioactive materials.*\\\\n\\\\n\\\&quot;)\&quot;}&quot;" files="" embeds="&quot;&quot;">

<details type="tool_calls" done="true" id="chatcmpl-tool-b7b8d15eddda57e7" name="docgen_write" arguments="&quot;{\&quot;request\&quot;: \&quot;{\\\&quot;format\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;pdf\\\&quot;, \\\&quot;filename\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;Radioactive Isotopes\\\&quot;, \\\&quot;content\\\&quot;: \\\&quot;# Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n\\\\n## A Comprehensive Guide\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Table of Contents\\\\n\\\\n1. Introduction to Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n2. Atomic Structure and Nuclear Stability\\\\n3. Types of Radioactive Decay\\\\n4. Half-Life and Decay Kinetics\\\\n5. Natural Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n6. Artificial (Synthetic) Radioisotopes\\\\n7. Radioisotopes in Medicine\\\\n8. Industrial and Agricultural Applications\\\\n9. Dating and Archaeology\\\\n10. Nuclear Power and Space Energy\\\\n11. Radiation Safety and Protection\\\\n12. Environmental Impact and Waste\\\\n13. Reference Table \\u2014 Key Radioisotopes\\\\n14. Glossary\\\\n15. Further Reading\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 1 \\u2014 Introduction\\\\n\\\\n## What Are Isotopes?\\\\n\\\\nEvery element is defined by its number of protons. Carbon always has 6. But carbon atoms can carry different numbers of neutrons. These variants are **isotopes**.\\\\n\\\\n- **Carbon-12** (6p, 6n) \\u2014 stable, most abundant\\\\n- **Carbon-13** (6p, 7n) \\u2014 stable, ~1.1% of natural carbon\\\\n- **Carbon-14** (6p, 8n) \\u2014 radioactive, trace amounts\\\\n\\\\n**Radioisotopes** (or **radionuclides**) are isotopes whose nuclei are unstable. They spontaneously break apart, releasing energy as radiation. Of roughly 3,300 known nuclides, only about 250\\u2013270 are stable \\u2014 the rest are radioactive.\\\\n\\\\n## The Origin of Radioactivity\\\\n\\\\nRadioactivity was discovered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel, who noticed uranium salts fogged photographic plates without any light source. Marie and Pierre Curie followed this with the discovery of polonium and radium, coining the term *radioactivity* from the Latin *radius* (ray).\\\\n\\\\nNuclei become unstable when the balance between the **strong nuclear force** (holding nucleons together) and **electromagnetic repulsion** (pushing protons apart) tips. Too many or too few neutrons relative to protons, or simply too many nucleons overall, leads to decay.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 2 \\u2014 Atomic Structure and Nuclear Stability\\\\n\\\\n## The Nucleus\\\\n\\\\nThe nucleus occupies less than one ten-thousandth of an atom&#x27;s diameter but contains over 99.9% of its mass. Nuclear density reaches approximately $2.3 \\\\\\\\times 10^{17}$ kg/m\\u00b3 \\u2014 a sugar cube of nuclear matter would weigh two hundred million tons.\\\\n\\\\n## Binding Energy\\\\n\\\\nWhen nucleons bind together, energy is released. The **binding energy** comes from the *mass defect*: the nucleus weighs slightly less than its individual protons and neutrons, with the missing mass converted via $E = mc^2$. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, making iron the most tightly bound element.\\\\n\\\\n## The Band of Stability\\\\n\\\\nLight elements have roughly equal protons and neutrons. Heavier elements need progressively more neutrons to offset proton repulsion. Beyond bismuth (Z = 83), **no stable isotopes exist** \\u2014 every isotope of polonium, radon, radium, uranium, plutonium, and beyond is radioactive.\\\\n\\\\n## Magic Numbers\\\\n\\\\nCertain nucleon counts \\u2014 **2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, and 126** \\u2014 confer extra stability, analogous to electron shell closures. Nuclei with magic proton and neutron counts (e.g., helium-4, oxygen-16, lead-208) are **doubly magic** and exceptionally stable.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 3 \\u2014 Types of Radioactive Decay\\\\n\\\\n## Alpha ($\\\\\\\\alpha$) Decay\\\\n\\\\nA heavy nucleus ejects a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons):\\\\n\\\\n$$^{238}_{92}\\\\\\\\text{U} \\\\\\\\rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\\\\\\\\text{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\\\\\\\\text{He}$$\\\\n\\\\nAlpha particles are heavy, slow, and doubly charged. They are stopped by paper or skin, but if inhaled they are extremely damaging.\\\\n\\\\n## Beta ($\\\\\\\\beta$) Decay\\\\n\\\\nThe weak nuclear force changes a neutron into a proton (or vice versa).\\\\n\\\\n**Beta-minus ($\\\\\\\\beta^-$):** A neutron \\u2192 proton + electron + antineutrino\\\\n$$^{14}_{6}\\\\\\\\text{C} \\\\\\\\rightarrow {}^{14}_{7}\\\\\\\\text{N} + e^- + \\\\\\\\bar{\\\\\\\\nu}_e$$\\\\n\\\\n**Beta-plus ($\\\\\\\\beta^+$) / Positron Emission:** A proton \\u2192 neutron + positron + neutrino\\\\n$$^{22}_{11}\\\\\\\\text{Na} \\\\\\\\rightarrow {}^{22}_{10}\\\\\\\\text{Ne} + e^+ + \\\\\\\\nu_e$$\\\\n\\\\nBeta particles are moderately penetrating, stopped by a few millimeters of aluminum.\\\\n\\\\n## Gamma ($\\\\\\\\gamma$) Decay\\\\n\\\\nHigh-energy photons emitted when an excited nucleus drops to a lower energy state, often accompanying alpha or beta decay. Gamma rays are highly penetrating, requiring thick lead or meters of concrete for shielding.\\\\n\\\\n## Electron Capture\\\\n\\\\nA nucleus captures one of its own inner electrons, converting a proton to a neutron. This leaves a vacancy in the inner electron shell, producing characteristic X-rays.\\\\n\\\\n## Spontaneous Fission\\\\n\\\\nVery heavy nuclei (e.g., californium-252) can split into two roughly equal fragments, releasing free neutrons and enormous energy \\u2014 the same process used in nuclear weapons and reactors.\\\\n\\\\n| Decay Type | Particle | Charge | Penetration | Stopped By |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Alpha ($\\\\\\\\alpha$) | Helium nucleus | +2 | Very low | Paper, skin |\\\\n| Beta-minus ($\\\\\\\\beta^-$) | Electron | -1 | Moderate | Aluminum foil |\\\\n| Beta-plus ($\\\\\\\\beta^+$) | Positron | +1 | Moderate | Aluminum foil |\\\\n| Gamma ($\\\\\\\\gamma$) | Photon | 0 | Very high | Lead, concrete |\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 4 \\u2014 Half-Life and Decay Kinetics\\\\n\\\\n## The Half-Life\\\\n\\\\nThe **half-life** ($t_{1/2}$) is the time for half of a sample to decay. It is fixed for each isotope, unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical state.\\\\n\\\\n- **Polonium-214**: 164 microseconds\\\\n- **Iodine-131**: 8.02 days\\\\n- **Carbon-14**: 5,730 years\\\\n- **Uranium-238**: 4.47 billion years\\\\n- **Tellurium-128**: $2.2 \\\\\\\\times 10^{24}$ years (longer than the universe)\\\\n\\\\n## The Decay Law\\\\n\\\\n$$N(t) = N_0 \\\\\\\\cdot \\\\\\\\left(\\\\\\\\frac{1}{2}\\\\\\\\right)^{t / t_{1/2}}$$\\\\n\\\\n**Activity** ($A$) is decays per second, measured in **becquerels (Bq)**. The older unit, the **curie (Ci)** = $3.7 \\\\\\\\times 10^{10}$ Bq.\\\\n\\\\n## Decay Chains\\\\n\\\\nMany isotopes decay through a chain of intermediates. Uranium-238 undergoes 14 steps (8 alpha + 6 beta decays) before reaching stable lead-206. At **secular equilibrium**, the activity of each chain member equals the parent&#x27;s activity.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 5 \\u2014 Natural Radioactive Isotopes\\\\n\\\\n## Primordial Radionuclides\\\\n\\\\nFormed in supernovae before the solar system, surviving due to extremely long half-lives:\\\\n\\\\n- **Uranium-238** ($t_{1/2}$ = 4.47 billion years) \\u2192 uranium series\\\\n- **Uranium-235** ($t_{1/2}$ = 704 million years) \\u2192 actinium series\\\\n- **Thorium-232** ($t_{1/2}$ = 14.05 billion years) \\u2192 thorium series\\\\n- **Potassium-40** ($t_{1/2}$ = 1.25 billion years) \\u2014 in all living things, in bananas, in granite\\\\n- **Rubidium-87** ($t_{1/2}$ = 48.8 billion years)\\\\n\\\\n## Cosmogenic Radionuclides\\\\n\\\\nProduced continuously by cosmic rays striking the atmosphere:\\\\n\\\\n- **Carbon-14** \\u2014 cosmic-ray neutrons hit nitrogen-14\\\\n- **Tritium (H-3)** \\u2014 neutron capture on lithium\\\\n- **Beryllium-10** \\u2014 upper atmosphere, used in geological dating\\\\n\\\\n## Radiogenic Radionuclides\\\\n\\\\nDecay products of primordial isotopes:\\\\n\\\\n- **Radon-222** \\u2014 colorless radioactive gas from radium-226; accumulates in homes, second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking\\\\n- **Polonium-210** \\u2014 part of uranium-238 chain, highly toxic\\\\n\\\\n## Background Radiation\\\\n\\\\nEveryone receives natural radiation continuously:\\\\n\\\\n| Source | Approx. Annual Dose |\\\\n|---|---|\\\\n| Cosmic radiation | ~0.4 mSv |\\\\n| Terrestrial (soil, rock) | ~0.5 mSv |\\\\n| Internal (K-40, C-14 in body) | ~0.3 mSv |\\\\n| Radon inhalation | ~1.2 mSv |\\\\n| **Total (global average)** | **~2.4 mSv/year** |\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 6 \\u2014 Artificial Radioisotopes\\\\n\\\\n## Production Methods\\\\n\\\\n### Nuclear Reactors\\\\nNeutrons from fission bombard target materials, inducing neutron capture:\\\\n- Cobalt-59 \\u2192 Cobalt-60\\\\n- Iodine isotopes from tellurium targets\\\\n- Tritium from lithium targets\\\\n\\\\n### Particle Accelerators (Cyclotrons)\\\\nCharged particles strike target nuclei at high energy:\\\\n- Fluorine-18 (for PET scans) from oxygen-18 + protons\\\\n- Technetium-99m precursors\\\\n- Indium-111 for imaging\\\\n\\\\n### Fission Product Separation\\\\nFission of U-235 or Pu-239 produces neutron-rich isotopes separated from spent fuel:\\\\n- Cesium-137, Strontium-90, Iodine-131\\\\n\\\\n## Transuranic Elements\\\\n\\\\nAll elements beyond uranium (Z &gt; 92) are synthetic and radioactive.\\\\n\\\\n| Element | Z | Discovery | Key Isotope |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Neptunium | 93 | 1940 | Np-237 |\\\\n| Plutonium | 94 | 1940 | Pu-239 |\\\\n| Americium | 95 | 1944 | Am-241 |\\\\n| Californium | 98 | 1950 | Cf-252 |\\\\n\\\\nThe heaviest (up to oganesson, Z = 118) have half-lives measured in milliseconds.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 7 \\u2014 Radioisotopes in Medicine\\\\n\\\\n## Diagnostic Imaging\\\\n\\\\n### Technetium-99m ($t_{1/2}$ = 6 hours)\\\\nUsed in ~80% of diagnostic nuclear imaging. Emits a 140 keV gamma ray ideal for detection, with no accompanying beta radiation. Chelated to different molecules, it images heart, bones, lungs, kidneys, and brain.\\\\n\\\\n### Fluorine-18 ($t_{1/2}$ = 110 minutes)\\\\nKey isotope in **PET scans**. Attached to glucose as FDG, it reveals areas of high metabolic activity \\u2014 including cancerous tumors.\\\\n\\\\n### Iodine-123 ($t_{1/2}$ = 13.2 hours)\\\\nImages and assesses thyroid function.\\\\n\\\\n## Radiation Therapy\\\\n\\\\n### Iodine-131 ($t_{1/2}$ = 8 days)\\\\nOrally administered to destroy overactive thyroid tissue or thyroid cancer.\\\\n\\\\n### Cobalt-60 ($t_{1/2}$ = 5.27 years)\\\\nExternal beam radiation therapy machine, still used widely in developing countries.\\\\n\\\\n### Brachytherapy\\\\nSealed sources placed inside or beside tumors:\\\\n- **Iridium-192** \\u2014 breast, cervix, prostate cancer\\\\n- **Iodine-125** \\u2014 permanent seeds for prostate cancer\\\\n- **Radium-223** \\u2014 alpha-emitter for bone metastases\\\\n\\\\n## Sterilization\\\\n\\\\nCobalt-60 gamma sources sterilize medical equipment (syringes, gloves, sutures, implants). Over 40% of single-use medical devices worldwide are sterilized this way.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 8 \\u2014 Industrial and Agricultural Applications\\\\n\\\\n## Industry\\\\n\\\\n- **Radiography**: Gamma sources (Ir-192, Co-60) inspect welds, pipelines, and castings for internal flaws\\\\n- **Thickness gauges**: Beta or gamma sources measure material thickness in real time (paper mills, steel mills)\\\\n- **Smoke detectors**: Americium-241 (alpha emitter) ionizes air \\u2014 smoke disrupts the current. ~1 billion detectors contain Am-241\\\\n- **Tracers**: Trace fluid flow through pipelines and detect leaks\\\\n\\\\n## Agriculture\\\\n\\\\n- **Mutation breeding**: Cobalt-60 gamma rays induce mutations; thousands of improved crop varieties developed\\\\n- **Sterile insect technique**: Males sterilized with radiation and released; wild population crashes. Eradicated screwworm from the Americas\\\\n- **Food irradiation**: Low-dose gamma or electron beams kill bacteria and parasites without making food radioactive\\\\n- **Fertilizer studies**: Phosphorus-32 tracks nutrient uptake in plants\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 9 \\u2014 Dating and Archaeology\\\\n\\\\n## Carbon-14 Dating\\\\n\\\\nDiscovered by Willard Libby (1949). Living organisms maintain a steady C-14/C-12 ratio through atmospheric exchange. At death, C-14 decays ($t_{1/2}$ = 5,730 years).\\\\n\\\\n$$\\\\\\\\text{Age} = -\\\\\\\\frac{t_{1/2}}{\\\\\\\\ln(2)} \\\\\\\\cdot \\\\\\\\ln\\\\\\\\left(\\\\\\\\frac{N}{N_0}\\\\\\\\right)$$\\\\n\\\\nReliable up to ~50,000\\u201360,000 years. Requires calibration using tree-ring data.\\\\n\\\\n## Other Dating Methods\\\\n\\\\n| Method | Isotope | Half-Life | Range |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Radiocarbon | C-14 | 5,730 y | Up to ~50 ka |\\\\n| Potassium-Argon | K-40 | 1.25 billion y | 100 ka \\u2013 4.5 Ga |\\\\n| Uranium-Lead | U-238 | 4.47 billion y | Millions \\u2013 billions y |\\\\n| Rubidium-Strontium | Rb-87 | 48.8 billion y | Billions y |\\\\n| Beryllium-10 | Be-10 | 1.39 million y | Exposure dating |\\\\n\\\\nUranium-lead dating of zircon crystals dated the Earth at ~4.54 billion years. Potassium-argon dating is essential for early hominin sites in East Africa.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 10 \\u2014 Nuclear Power and Space Energy\\\\n\\\\n## Fission Power\\\\n\\\\nUranium-235 and plutonium-239 fission releases ~200 MeV per event \\u2014 a million times the energy of a chemical reaction. Natural uranium contains only 0.7% U-235; most reactors require enrichment to 3\\u20135%.\\\\n\\\\n## Breeder Reactors\\\\n\\\\nConvert fertile isotopes (U-238, Th-232) into fissile fuel (Pu-239, U-233), potentially extending uranium resources 60-fold. Thorium is abundant but largely experimental.\\\\n\\\\n## RTGs \\u2014 Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators\\\\n\\\\n**Plutonium-238** ($t_{1/2}$ = 87.7 years, alpha emitter) powers:\\\\n- Voyager 1 and 2 (launched 1977, still operating at 15+ billion km)\\\\n- New Horizons (Pluto flyby 2015)\\\\n- Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers\\\\n- Deep Space 1, Cassini, Galileo\\\\n\\\\nRTGs operate for decades where solar panels are impractical: deep space, Martian winter, or the Moon&#x27;s dark side.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 11 \\u2014 Radiation Safety and Protection\\\\n\\\\n## Dose Units\\\\n\\\\n| Quantity | Unit | Description |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| Activity | Bq | Decays per second |\\\\n| Absorbed dose | Gy | Energy per kg (1 Gy = 1 J/kg) |\\\\n| Equivalent dose | Sv | Absorbed dose \\u00d7 radiation weight |\\\\n| Effective dose | Sv | Equivalent dose \\u00d7 tissue weight |\\\\n\\\\n## Typical Doses\\\\n\\\\n| Source | Effective Dose |\\\\n|---|---|\\\\n| Background (annual) | ~2.4 mSv |\\\\n| Chest X-ray | 0.1 mSv |\\\\n| CT scan (abdomen) | ~10 mSv |\\\\n| Cross-country flight | 0.1 mSv |\\\\n| Worker annual limit | 50 mSv |\\\\n| Radiation sickness threshold | ~1 Sv |\\\\n| Lethal dose (LD50) | ~3.5\\u20134 Sv |\\\\n\\\\n## ALARA Principle\\\\n\\\\n**As Low As Reasonably Achievable** \\u2014 three practical rules:\\\\n1. **Time** \\u2014 minimize exposure duration\\\\n2. **Distance** \\u2014 intensity falls with the square of distance\\\\n3. **Shielding** \\u2014 interpose appropriate material (lead for gamma, plastic for beta, water/concrete for neutrons)\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 12 \\u2014 Environmental Impact and Waste\\\\n\\\\n## Waste Categories\\\\n\\\\n| Category | Examples | Disposal |\\\\n|---|---|---|\\\\n| Low-level | Gloves, tools, filters | Near-surface |\\\\n| Intermediate | Resins, sludges | Concrete, intermediate depth |\\\\n| High-level | Spent nuclear fuel | Deep geological repository |\\\\n| Transuranic | Pu-bearing materials | Deep disposal (e.g., WIPP) |\\\\n\\\\n## Spent Fuel\\\\n\\\\n~10,000\\u201312,000 tons produced annually worldwide. Remains highly radioactive for thousands of years. Finland&#x27;s Onkalo repository (expected ~2025) is the first deep geological repository.\\\\n\\\\n## Major Disasters\\\\n\\\\n| Event | Year | Cause | Impact |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Three Mile Island | 1979 | Partial meltdown | No deaths, shaped US policy |\\\\n| Chernobyl | 1986 | Design flaw + operator error | ~6 million exposed; worst nuclear disaster |\\\\n| Fukushima | 2011 | Earthquake + tsunami | 3 meltdowns; partial evacuation |\\\\n\\\\n## Weapons Legacy\\\\n\\\\nAtmospheric testing (1945\\u20131980) dispersed strontium-90 and cesium-137 worldwide. Some test sites (Nevada, Semipalatinsk) remain contaminated.\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 13 \\u2014 Key Radioisotopes Reference\\\\n\\\\n| Isotope | Half-Life | Decay | Key Uses |\\\\n|---|---|---|---|\\\\n| Tritium (H-3) | 12.3 y | \\u03b2\\u207b | Luminous sights, fusion research |\\\\n| Carbon-14 | 5,730 y | \\u03b2\\u207b | Radiocarbon dating |\\\\n| Potassium-40 | 1.25 billion y | \\u03b2\\u207b, EC | Geological dating, background |\\\\n| Cobalt-60 | 5.27 y | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Cancer therapy, sterilization |\\\\n| Cesium-137 | 30.17 y | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Medical therapy, gauges |\\\\n| Strontium-90 | 28.8 y | \\u03b2\\u207b | RTGs, bone palliation |\\\\n| Iodine-131 | 8.02 d | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Thyroid treatment |\\\\n| Technetium-99m | 6 h | \\u03b3 | Diagnostic imaging |\\\\n| Americium-241 | 432.2 y | \\u03b1 + \\u03b3 | Smoke detectors |\\\\n| Plutonium-238 | 87.7 y | \\u03b1 | RTGs for space |\\\\n| Plutonium-239 | 24,110 y | \\u03b1 | Weapons, reactor fuel |\\\\n| Radium-226 | 1,600 y | \\u03b1 + \\u03b3 | Historical luminescent paint |\\\\n| Radon-222 | 3.82 d | \\u03b1 | Indoor air hazard |\\\\n| Polonium-210 | 138.4 d | \\u03b1 | Static eliminators |\\\\n| Californium-252 | 2.645 y | \\u03b1, SF | Neutron source |\\\\n| Uranium-235 | 704 million y | \\u03b1 | Nuclear fuel, weapons |\\\\n| Fluorine-18 | 110 min | \\u03b2\\u207a | PET imaging |\\\\n\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Chapter 14 \\u2014 Glossary\\\\n\\\\n**Activity** \\u2014 Nuclear decays per unit time (becquerels).\\\\n\\\\n**Alpha particle** \\u2014 Helium-4 nucleus (2p, 2n) emitted in alpha decay.\\\\n\\\\n**Band of stability** \\u2014 Region on the N vs. Z chart where stable nuclides lie.\\\\n\\\\n**Becquerel (Bq)** \\u2014 SI unit of activity; one decay per second.\\\\n\\\\n**Binding energy** \\u2014 Energy to disassemble a nucleus into free nucleons.\\\\n\\\\n**Curie (Ci)** \\u2014 $3.7 \\\\\\\\times 10^{10}$ Bq (activity of 1 g radium-226).\\\\n\\\\n**Decay chain** \\u2014 Successive decays from parent to stable product.\\\\n\\\\n**Gray (Gy)** \\u2014 SI unit of absorbed dose; <details type="tool_calls" done="true" id="chatcmpl-tool-bb09dc6de3dd7de1" name="write_file" arguments="&quot;{\&quot;content\&quot;: \&quot;# Radioactive Isotopes\\n\\n## A Comprehensive Guide\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Table of Contents\\n\\n1. Introduction to Radioactive Isotopes\\n2. Atomic Structure and Nuclear Stability\\n3. Types of Radioactive Decay\\n4. Half-Life and Decay Kinetics\\n5. Natural Radioactive Isotopes\\n6. Artificial (Synthetic) Radioisotopes\\n7. Radioisotopes in Medicine\\n8. Industrial and Agricultural Applications\\n9. Dating and Archaeology\\n10. Nuclear Power and Space Energy\\n11. Radiation Safety and Protection\\n12. Environmental Impact and Waste\\n13. Reference Table \\u2014 Key Radioisotopes\\n14. Glossary\\n15. Further Reading\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 1 \\u2014 Introduction\\n\\n## What Are Isotopes?\\n\\nEvery element is defined by its number of protons. Carbon always has 6. But carbon atoms can carry different numbers of neutrons. These variants are **isotopes**.\\n\\n- **Carbon-12** (6p, 6n) \\u2014 stable, most abundant\\n- **Carbon-13** (6p, 7n) \\u2014 stable, ~1.1% of natural carbon\\n- **Carbon-14** (6p, 8n) \\u2014 radioactive, trace amounts\\n\\n**Radioisotopes** (or **radionuclides**) are isotopes whose nuclei are unstable. They spontaneously break apart, releasing energy as radiation. Of roughly 3,300 known nuclides, only about 250\\u2013270 are stable \\u2014 the rest are radioactive.\\n\\n## The Origin of Radioactivity\\n\\nRadioactivity was discovered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel, who noticed uranium salts fogged photographic plates without any light source. Marie and Pierre Curie followed this with the discovery of polonium and radium, coining the term *radioactivity* from the Latin *radius* (ray).\\n\\nNuclei become unstable when the balance between the **strong nuclear force** (holding nucleons together) and **electromagnetic repulsion** (pushing protons apart) tips. Too many or too few neutrons relative to protons, or simply too many nucleons overall, leads to decay.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 2 \\u2014 Atomic Structure and Nuclear Stability\\n\\n## The Nucleus\\n\\nThe nucleus occupies less than one ten-thousandth of an atom&#x27;s diameter but contains over 99.9% of its mass. Nuclear density reaches approximately 2.3 \\u00d7 10^17 kg/m\\u00b3 \\u2014 a sugar cube of nuclear matter would weigh two hundred million tons.\\n\\n## Binding Energy\\n\\nWhen nucleons bind together, energy is released. The **binding energy** comes from the *mass defect*: the nucleus weighs slightly less than its individual protons and neutrons, with the missing mass converted via E = mc\\u00b2. Binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, making iron the most tightly bound element.\\n\\n## The Band of Stability\\n\\nLight elements have roughly equal protons and neutrons. Heavier elements need progressively more neutrons to offset proton repulsion. Beyond bismuth (Z = 83), **no stable isotopes exist** \\u2014 every isotope of polonium, radon, radium, uranium, plutonium, and beyond is radioactive.\\n\\n## Magic Numbers\\n\\nCertain nucleon counts \\u2014 **2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, and 126** \\u2014 confer extra stability, analogous to electron shell closures. Nuclei with magic proton and neutron counts (e.g., helium-4, oxygen-16, lead-208) are **doubly magic** and exceptionally stable.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 3 \\u2014 Types of Radioactive Decay\\n\\n## Alpha (\\u03b1) Decay\\n\\nA heavy nucleus ejects a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons):\\n\\n    \\u00b2\\u00b3\\u2078\\u2089\\u2082U \\u2192 \\u00b2\\u00b3\\u2074\\u2089\\u2080Th + \\u2074\\u2082He\\n\\nAlpha particles are heavy, slow, and doubly charged. They are stopped by paper or skin, but if inhaled they are extremely damaging.\\n\\n## Beta (\\u03b2) Decay\\n\\nThe weak nuclear force changes a neutron into a proton (or vice versa).\\n\\n**Beta-minus (\\u03b2\\u207b):** A neutron \\u2192 proton + electron + antineutrino\\n    \\u00b9\\u2074\\u2086C \\u2192 \\u00b9\\u2074\\u2087N + e\\u207b + \\u03bd\\u0304\\u2091\\n\\n**Beta-plus (\\u03b2\\u207a) / Positron Emission:** A proton \\u2192 neutron + positron + neutrino\\n    \\u00b2\\u00b2\\u2081\\u2081Na \\u2192 \\u00b2\\u00b2\\u2081\\u2080Ne + e\\u207a + \\u03bd\\u2091\\n\\nBeta particles are moderately penetrating, stopped by a few millimeters of aluminum.\\n\\n## Gamma (\\u03b3) Decay\\n\\nHigh-energy photons emitted when an excited nucleus drops to a lower energy state, often accompanying alpha or beta decay. Gamma rays are highly penetrating, requiring thick lead or meters of concrete for shielding.\\n\\n## Electron Capture\\n\\nA nucleus captures one of its own inner electrons, converting a proton to a neutron. This leaves a vacancy in the inner electron shell, producing characteristic X-rays.\\n\\n## Spontaneous Fission\\n\\nVery heavy nuclei (e.g., californium-252) can split into two roughly equal fragments, releasing free neutrons and enormous energy \\u2014 the same process used in nuclear weapons and reactors.\\n\\n### Decay Comparison\\n\\n| Decay Type | Particle | Charge | Penetration | Stopped By |\\n|---|---|---|---|---|\\n| Alpha (\\u03b1) | Helium nucleus | +2 | Very low | Paper, skin |\\n| Beta-minus (\\u03b2\\u207b) | Electron | -1 | Moderate | Aluminum foil |\\n| Beta-plus (\\u03b2\\u207a) | Positron | +1 | Moderate | Aluminum foil |\\n| Gamma (\\u03b3) | Photon | 0 | Very high | Lead, concrete |\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 4 \\u2014 Half-Life and Decay Kinetics\\n\\n## The Half-Life\\n\\nThe **half-life** (t\\u2081/\\u2082) is the time for half of a sample to decay. It is fixed for each isotope, unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical state.\\n\\n- **Polonium-214**: 164 microseconds\\n- **Iodine-131**: 8.02 days\\n- **Carbon-14**: 5,730 years\\n- **Uranium-238**: 4.47 billion years\\n- **Tellurium-128**: 2.2 \\u00d7 10\\u00b2\\u2074 years (longer than the universe)\\n\\n## The Decay Law\\n\\n    N(t) = N\\u2080 \\u00d7 (1/2)^(t / t\\u2081/\\u2082)\\n\\n**Activity** (A) is decays per second, measured in **becquerels (Bq)**. The older unit, the **curie (Ci)** = 3.7 \\u00d7 10\\u00b9\\u2070 Bq.\\n\\n## Decay Chains\\n\\nMany isotopes decay through a chain of intermediates. Uranium-238 undergoes 14 steps (8 alpha + 6 beta decays) before reaching stable lead-206. At **secular equilibrium**, the activity of each chain member equals the parent&#x27;s activity.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 5 \\u2014 Natural Radioactive Isotopes\\n\\n## Primordial Radionuclides\\n\\nFormed in supernovae before the solar system, surviving due to extremely long half-lives:\\n\\n- **Uranium-238** (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 4.47 billion years) \\u2192 uranium series\\n- **Uranium-235** (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 704 million years) \\u2192 actinium series\\n- **Thorium-232** (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 14.05 billion years) \\u2192 thorium series\\n- **Potassium-40** (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 1.25 billion years) \\u2014 in all living things, in bananas, in granite\\n- **Rubidium-87** (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 48.8 billion years)\\n\\n## Cosmogenic Radionuclides\\n\\nProduced continuously by cosmic rays striking the atmosphere:\\n\\n- **Carbon-14** \\u2014 cosmic-ray neutrons hit nitrogen-14\\n- **Tritium (H-3)** \\u2014 neutron capture on lithium\\n- **Beryllium-10** \\u2014 upper atmosphere, used in geological dating\\n\\n## Radiogenic Radionuclides\\n\\nDecay products of primordial isotopes:\\n\\n- **Radon-222** \\u2014 colorless radioactive gas from radium-226; accumulates in homes, second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking\\n- **Polonium-210** \\u2014 part of uranium-238 chain, highly toxic\\n\\n## Background Radiation\\n\\nEveryone receives natural radiation continuously:\\n\\n| Source | Approx. Annual Dose |\\n|---|---|\\n| Cosmic radiation | ~0.4 mSv |\\n| Terrestrial (soil, rock) | ~0.5 mSv |\\n| Internal (K-40, C-14 in body) | ~0.3 mSv |\\n| Radon inhalation | ~1.2 mSv |\\n| **Total (global average)** | **~2.4 mSv/year** |\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 6 \\u2014 Artificial Radioisotopes\\n\\n## Production Methods\\n\\n### Nuclear Reactors\\nNeutrons from fission bombard target materials, inducing neutron capture:\\n- Cobalt-59 \\u2192 Cobalt-60\\n- Iodine isotopes from tellurium targets\\n- Tritium from lithium targets\\n\\n### Particle Accelerators (Cyclotrons)\\nCharged particles strike target nuclei at high energy:\\n- Fluorine-18 (for PET scans) from oxygen-18 + protons\\n- Technetium-99m precursors\\n- Indium-111 for imaging\\n\\n### Fission Product Separation\\nFission of U-235 or Pu-239 produces neutron-rich isotopes separated from spent fuel:\\n- Cesium-137, Strontium-90, Iodine-131\\n\\n## Transuranic Elements\\n\\nAll elements beyond uranium (Z &gt; 92) are synthetic and radioactive.\\n\\n| Element | Z | Discovery | Key Isotope |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| Neptunium | 93 | 1940 | Np-237 |\\n| Plutonium | 94 | 1940 | Pu-239 |\\n| Americium | 95 | 1944 | Am-241 |\\n| Californium | 98 | 1950 | Cf-252 |\\n\\nThe heaviest (up to oganesson, Z = 118) have half-lives measured in milliseconds.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 7 \\u2014 Radioisotopes in Medicine\\n\\n## Diagnostic Imaging\\n\\n### Technetium-99m (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 6 hours)\\nUsed in ~80% of diagnostic nuclear imaging. Emits a 140 keV gamma ray ideal for detection, with no accompanying beta radiation. Chelated to different molecules, it images heart, bones, lungs, kidneys, and brain.\\n\\n### Fluorine-18 (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 110 minutes)\\nKey isotope in **PET scans**. Attached to glucose as FDG, it reveals areas of high metabolic activity \\u2014 including cancerous tumors.\\n\\n### Iodine-123 (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 13.2 hours)\\nImages and assesses thyroid function.\\n\\n## Radiation Therapy\\n\\n### Iodine-131 (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 8 days)\\nOrally administered to destroy overactive thyroid tissue or thyroid cancer.\\n\\n### Cobalt-60 (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 5.27 years)\\nExternal beam radiation therapy machine, still used widely in developing countries.\\n\\n### Brachytherapy\\nSealed sources placed inside or beside tumors:\\n- **Iridium-192** \\u2014 breast, cervix, prostate cancer\\n- **Iodine-125** \\u2014 permanent seeds for prostate cancer\\n- **Radium-223** \\u2014 alpha-emitter for bone metastases\\n\\n## Sterilization\\n\\nCobalt-60 gamma sources sterilize medical equipment (syringes, gloves, sutures, implants). Over 40% of single-use medical devices worldwide are sterilized this way.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 8 \\u2014 Industrial and Agricultural Applications\\n\\n## Industry\\n\\n- **Radiography**: Gamma sources (Ir-192, Co-60) inspect welds, pipelines, and castings for internal flaws\\n- **Thickness gauges**: Beta or gamma sources measure material thickness in real time (paper mills, steel mills)\\n- **Smoke detectors**: Americium-241 (alpha emitter) ionizes air \\u2014 smoke disrupts the current. ~1 billion detectors contain Am-241\\n- **Tracers**: Trace fluid flow through pipelines and detect leaks\\n\\n## Agriculture\\n\\n- **Mutation breeding**: Cobalt-60 gamma rays induce mutations; thousands of improved crop varieties developed\\n- **Sterile insect technique**: Males sterilized with radiation and released; wild population crashes. Eradicated screwworm from the Americas\\n- **Food irradiation**: Low-dose gamma or electron beams kill bacteria and parasites without making food radioactive\\n- **Fertilizer studies**: Phosphorus-32 tracks nutrient uptake in plants\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 9 \\u2014 Dating and Archaeology\\n\\n## Carbon-14 Dating\\n\\nDiscovered by Willard Libby (1949). Living organisms maintain a steady C-14/C-12 ratio through atmospheric exchange. At death, C-14 decays (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 5,730 years).\\n\\nReliable up to ~50,000\\u201360,000 years. Requires calibration using tree-ring data.\\n\\n## Other Dating Methods\\n\\n| Method | Isotope | Half-Life | Range |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| Radiocarbon | C-14 | 5,730 y | Up to ~50 ka |\\n| Potassium-Argon | K-40 | 1.25 billion y | 100 ka \\u2013 4.5 Ga |\\n| Uranium-Lead | U-238 | 4.47 billion y | Millions \\u2013 billions y |\\n| Rubidium-Strontium | Rb-87 | 48.8 billion y | Billions y |\\n| Beryllium-10 | Be-10 | 1.39 million y | Exposure dating |\\n\\nUranium-lead dating of zircon crystals dated the Earth at ~4.54 billion years. Potassium-argon dating is essential for early hominin sites in East Africa.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 10 \\u2014 Nuclear Power and Space Energy\\n\\n## Fission Power\\n\\nUranium-235 and plutonium-239 fission releases ~200 MeV per event \\u2014 a million times the energy of a chemical reaction. Natural uranium contains only 0.7% U-235; most reactors require enrichment to 3\\u20135%.\\n\\n## Breeder Reactors\\n\\nConvert fertile isotopes (U-238, Th-232) into fissile fuel (Pu-239, U-233), potentially extending uranium resources 60-fold. Thorium is abundant but largely experimental.\\n\\n## RTGs \\u2014 Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generators\\n\\n**Plutonium-238** (t\\u2081/\\u2082 = 87.7 years, alpha emitter) powers:\\n- Voyager 1 and 2 (launched 1977, still operating at 15+ billion km)\\n- New Horizons (Pluto flyby 2015)\\n- Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers\\n- Deep Space 1, Cassini, Galileo\\n\\nRTGs operate for decades where solar panels are impractical: deep space, Martian winter, or the Moon&#x27;s dark side.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 11 \\u2014 Radiation Safety and Protection\\n\\n## Dose Units\\n\\n| Quantity | Unit | Description |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| Activity | Bq | Decays per second |\\n| Absorbed dose | Gy | Energy per kg (1 Gy = 1 J/kg) |\\n| Equivalent dose | Sv | Absorbed dose \\u00d7 radiation weight |\\n| Effective dose | Sv | Equivalent dose \\u00d7 tissue weight |\\n\\n## Typical Doses\\n\\n| Source | Effective Dose |\\n|---|---|\\n| Background (annual) | ~2.4 mSv |\\n| Chest X-ray | 0.1 mSv |\\n| CT scan (abdomen) | ~10 mSv |\\n| Cross-country flight | 0.1 mSv |\\n| Worker annual limit | 50 mSv |\\n| Radiation sickness threshold | ~1 Sv |\\n| Lethal dose (LD50) | ~3.5\\u20134 Sv |\\n\\n## ALARA Principle\\n\\n**As Low As Reasonably Achievable** \\u2014 three practical rules:\\n1. **Time** \\u2014 minimize exposure duration\\n2. **Distance** \\u2014 intensity falls with the square of distance\\n3. **Shielding** \\u2014 interpose appropriate material (lead for gamma, plastic for beta, water/concrete for neutrons)\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 12 \\u2014 Environmental Impact and Waste\\n\\n## Waste Categories\\n\\n| Category | Examples | Disposal |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| Low-level | Gloves, tools, filters | Near-surface |\\n| Intermediate | Resins, sludges | Concrete, intermediate depth |\\n| High-level | Spent nuclear fuel | Deep geological repository |\\n| Transuranic | Pu-bearing materials | Deep disposal (e.g., WIPP) |\\n\\n## Spent Fuel\\n\\n~10,000\\u201312,000 tons produced annually worldwide. Remains highly radioactive for thousands of years. Finland&#x27;s Onkalo repository (expected ~2025) is the first deep geological repository.\\n\\n## Major Disasters\\n\\n| Event | Year | Cause | Impact |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| Three Mile Island | 1979 | Partial meltdown | No deaths, shaped US policy |\\n| Chernobyl | 1986 | Design flaw + operator error | ~6 million exposed; worst nuclear disaster |\\n| Fukushima | 2011 | Earthquake + tsunami | 3 meltdowns; partial evacuation |\\n\\n## Weapons Legacy\\n\\nAtmospheric testing (1945\\u20131980) dispersed strontium-90 and cesium-137 worldwide. Some test sites (Nevada, Semipalatinsk) remain contaminated.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 13 \\u2014 Key Radioisotopes Reference\\n\\n| Isotope | Half-Life | Decay | Key Uses |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| Tritium (H-3) | 12.3 y | \\u03b2\\u207b | Luminous sights, fusion research |\\n| Carbon-14 | 5,730 y | \\u03b2\\u207b | Radiocarbon dating |\\n| Potassium-40 | 1.25 billion y | \\u03b2\\u207b, EC | Geological dating, background |\\n| Cobalt-60 | 5.27 y | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Cancer therapy, sterilization |\\n| Cesium-137 | 30.17 y | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Medical therapy, gauges |\\n| Strontium-90 | 28.8 y | \\u03b2\\u207b | RTGs, bone palliation |\\n| Iodine-131 | 8.02 d | \\u03b2\\u207b + \\u03b3 | Thyroid treatment |\\n| Technetium-99m | 6 h | \\u03b3 | Diagnostic imaging |\\n| Americium-241 | 432.2 y | \\u03b1 + \\u03b3 | Smoke detectors |\\n| Plutonium-238 | 87.7 y | \\u03b1 | RTGs for space |\\n| Plutonium-239 | 24,110 y | \\u03b1 | Weapons, reactor fuel |\\n| Radium-226 | 1,600 y | \\u03b1 + \\u03b3 | Historical luminescent paint |\\n| Radon-222 | 3.82 d | \\u03b1 | Indoor air hazard |\\n| Polonium-210 | 138.4 d | \\u03b1 | Static eliminators |\\n| Californium-252 | 2.645 y | \\u03b1, SF | Neutron source |\\n| Uranium-235 | 704 million y | \\u03b1 | Nuclear fuel, weapons |\\n| Fluorine-18 | 110 min | \\u03b2\\u207a | PET imaging |\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 14 \\u2014 Glossary\\n\\n**Activity** \\u2014 Nuclear decays per unit time (becquerels).\\n\\n**Alpha particle** \\u2014 Helium-4 nucleus (2p, 2n) emitted in alpha decay.\\n\\n**Band of stability** \\u2014 Region on the N vs. Z chart where stable nuclides lie.\\n\\n**Becquerel (Bq)** \\u2014 SI unit of activity; one decay per second.\\n\\n**Binding energy** \\u2014 Energy to disassemble a nucleus into free nucleons.\\n\\n**Brachytherapy** \\u2014 Radiation therapy using sealed sources placed inside or adjacent to the target tissue.\\n\\n**Curie (Ci)** \\u2014 3.7 \\u00d7 10\\u00b9\\u2070 Bq (activity of 1 g radium-226).\\n\\n**Decay chain** \\u2014 Successive decays from parent to stable product.\\n\\n**Effective dose** \\u2014 A weighted sum of equivalent doses to different tissues, measured in sieverts.\\n\\n**Fission** \\u2014 The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy.\\n\\n**Fusion** \\u2014 The combining of light nuclei into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.\\n\\n**Gray (Gy)** \\u2014 SI unit of absorbed dose; 1 J/kg.\\n\\n**Half-life** \\u2014 Time for half a radioactive sample to decay.\\n\\n**Isotope** \\u2014 Same element, different neutron count.\\n\\n**Radioisotope / Radionuclide** \\u2014 A radioactive isotope.\\n\\n**Sievert (Sv)** \\u2014 SI unit of equivalent/effective dose.\\n\\n**Strong nuclear force** \\u2014 Fundamental force binding nucleons together.\\n\\n**Transmutation** \\u2014 Converting one element/isotope into another through nuclear reactions.\\n\\n---\\n\\n# Chapter 15 \\u2014 Further Reading\\n\\n**Books:**\\n- *Atoms for Peace and War* \\u2014 John M. McPhee\\n- *The Making of the Atomic Bomb* \\u2014 Richard Rhodes\\n- *Nuclear Physics: Principles and Applications* \\u2014 John S. M.
